confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.

catalog_locator: §3.4 'Stress', pp. 88-91 (rule pp. 88-89, generalization p. 91); weight definition end of §3.3 (p. 87); restated §6.1 'The couplet and stress', pp. 209-211.
catalog_quote: Every IM lexical word must have one and only one primary stress, thus meeting the obligatoriness and culminativity requirements of Hyman’s (2006:231) definition of a stress accent language. [...] Stress is always located within a two syllable window of the right edge of the grammatical word—that is, on the couplet of the word. In words which end in a light syllable, stress is always on the the penultimate syllable—that is, on the first syllable of the disyllabic couplet, as shown in (89). [...] However, in words that surface with a heavy final syllable, stress is always on this syllable, as the examples in (90) show. [...] It should be noted that heavy syllables only occur as the final syllable of the grammatical word except occasionally in compounds where the initial member of the compound is a root with the surface form CV(ˀ)V [...] As a result, there are no lexical words with the forms *ˈCVː.CV or *ˈCVCVː. [...] The generalization that can be made about the location of stress on surface forms, then, is that, while the location is variable in terms of syllables (i.e. either an ultimate heavy syllable or penultimate light syllable), it always occurs on the initial mora of the final couplet of the word, or in other words, within a two mora window of the right edge of the grammatical word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per lexical word, on the penultimate mora of the grammatical word: the head of a single right-aligned moraic trochee (the Mixtec 'couplet'). This is the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is light (CV.CV couplet) and the final syllable when it is heavy/bimoraic (CVV couplet). Pre-couplet prefixal syllables are unfooted and never stressed; enclitics attach outside the foot and do not shift stress. Stress placement is independent of tone (IM is also tonal, 3 surface levels).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author states (p. 91) 'I also make the somewhat less emphatic claim that IM does not have secondary stress'; allows that unreduced compounds may contain two prosodic words and hence possibly a second stress; no instrumental study.
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy syllables occur only word-finally (occasionally non-finally in unreduced compounds whose first member is CV(ˀ)V); enclitics (=ɾà, =tʃì etc.) added after the grammatical word do not attract or shift stress; acoustic correlates only impressionistic (duration, consonant lengthening, intensity, precise articulation), 'lacking systematic instrumental study'. Spanish loans are adapted to a left-headed bimoraic foot (sec. 6.5).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the grammatical word (root/couplet plus prefixes), excluding postlexical enclitics; foot aligned to right edge of grammatical word inside the prosodic word. Tonal language with stress statement: stress and tone described as mutually independent. In moraic terms the rule is fixed penultimate-mora; in syllable terms penult~final depending on final-syllable weight (could also be coded weight-sensitive within a final two-syllable window).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ixtayutla Mixtec (ISO vmj, glottocode ixta1235) as spoken in the municipality of Santiago Ixtayutla, SW Oaxaca (East Coast Mixtec grouping per Josserand 1983); fieldwork consultants from Ixtayutla. Exact match to the target languoid.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 (pp. 88-92) and 6.1 (pp. 209-213): one obligatory, culminative primary stress per lexical word; stress falls on the initial mora of the word-final bimoraic couplet (= moraic trochee aligned to right edge of grammatical word): penultimate syllable if final syllable is light, final syllable if it is heavy (CVV); prefixes and enclitics do not shift stress; stress independent of tone; author claims no secondary stress (tentatively); Spanish loans adapted into left-headed bimoraic foot (6.5).
